title: Last words
hook: if la ilaha illallah is the whole point, why would anyone need to be prompted to say it?
tomorrow: who is the soul at peace, and when does it hear that call?

segments.voice: Yesterday: all settled. Ali handing back every deposit before he followed. When the things are settled, one question is left: the words.

Lists of famous last words get passed around online: funny ones, brave ones, strange ones. A hadith in Sunan Abu Dawud answers yesterday's question with one sentence: whoever's last words are la ilaha illallah, there is no god but Allah, enters Paradise. Simple enough. But a hadith in Sahih Muslim adds an odd instruction. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told people to prompt their dying with these words. Prompt them? If the sentence is the whole point, why would anyone need help saying it?
screen: `FAMOUS LAST WORDS.` → `LA ILAHA ILLALLAH.` → `WHY PROMPT IT?`

segments.voice: Because the end isn't always clear-headed. Pain, medicine, exhaustion, fear: the words you've said all your life can be hard to find at the door. So the people by the bed help. The word for this is talqin, prompting. And here's the second half of the puzzle. Scholars who wrote about it, such as al-Nawawi, advise saying it softly near the person, not ordering them to repeat it, and not pressing again once they've said it, unless they speak of other things. The prompt is a kindness, not a test. That's why the sentence is so short. La ilaha illallah is in the call to prayer, inside the prayer, in dhikr counted on the fingers. A life of saying it is a rehearsal, so that at the end it's already on the tongue. Some families say it quietly in a hospital room, not as an exam, but as company. In the hadith, then, the last words aren't left to chance. The people who love you help you find them.
screen: `THE END ISN'T CLEAR-HEADED.` · `TALQIN: A GENTLE PROMPT.` · `SOFTLY, AND DON'T PRESS.` · `A LIFE OF REHEARSAL.` · then, large: `MY LAST WORDS.`

segments.voice: Where you can, say la ilaha illallah softly, once, then again at the pace of your breath, listening to it instead of rushing. If you're learning about Islam rather than practicing it, simply listen to the shape of the words as someone else might say them, quietly, at a bedside.
screen: `SAY IT SOFTLY.` · `AT THE PACE OF YOUR BREATH.` · `LISTEN TO ITS SHAPE.`

segments.voice: Last words: the sentence a Muslim hopes to say at the end, la ilaha illallah, rehearsed over a lifetime and gently prompted by the people nearby.
Three words to keep: my last words, already practiced, already on the tongue. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims at the bedside of someone dying often say la ilaha illallah softly near them (talqin), without pressing them to repeat it; across life the phrase is said in the call to prayer, in prayer and in dhikr.

chat.says: Dadi says when it's her time, i shouldn't make her say anything. just sit close and say it myself. why?
options: That's talqin done gently: say it softly near her, as company, not a test she has to pass.
Because last words don't really count; only the deeds of her whole life are weighed at the end.
She's being modest. You're supposed to have her repeat it many times, to make sure it counts.
chat.meaning: The Prophet said to prompt the dying with la ilaha illallah; scholars advise doing it softly and not pressing. A kindness, not a test.

la ilaha illallah.meaning: there is no god but Allah

talqin.meaning: gently prompting the dying with la ilaha illallah

Sunan Abu Dawud.meaning: a major collection of reports of the Prophet's words and deeds

al-Nawawi.meaning: a medieval scholar who wrote on hadith and devotions

dhikr.meaning: remembering Allah, often by repeating short phrases

sources.ref: Sunan Abi Dawud 3116: whoever's last words are la ilaha illallah will enter Paradise
Sahih Muslim 916: prompt your dying with la ilaha illallah
al-Nawawi, al-Adhkar, on talqin: say it gently near the dying person, without pressing, and do not repeat once said unless they speak of other things

notes: Confirm Abu Dawud 3116 and Muslim 916 numbering and paraphrase.

Confirm the summary of al-Nawawi's advice in al-Adhkar on talqin (gentle, not insistent, not repeated once said unless the person speaks further). Schools differ on details (e.g. whether to include the second half of the shahada); the script keeps to the hadith's wording.
